As the very first submission in this subverse, I'd like to go over training one of the very first commands that people like to train their dogs. And that command is sit.

Some important things to remember when training any dog are: 1. Always keep training fun.

  1. Always end on a positive note.

  2. Vary the order in which you train commands to your dog. If you train the same commands in the same order, you may get a dog that begins to predict what command you'll work on next.

  3. Find what motivates your dog. This could be food, toys, attention or something else entirely!

  4. Only train for as long as you can keep your dog's attention. Doing several shorter training sessions in a day may be more successful for you and your dog than one longer session.

  5. Don't advance your criteria too quickly. Similarly, try not to linger too long on a step of your training.

So, for training a dog to sit using lure-reward, you'll need to have whatever motivates your dog. In this example, I will say my dog is food motivated.

Your first step when training sit using lure-reward is to use the command word that you are assigning the behavior (in this case "Sit") take the piece of food, hold the piece of food to your dog's nose, and move your hand upwards until your dog's butt hits the ground. When your dog's butt hits the ground, use a marker word (such as "Yes!") to mark that moment. This video shows this step, although the word "Sit" has been cut out. You will want to repeat this step 6-12 times.

The second step is to remove your lure, and transition to only the hand signal. Instead of holding the food to your dog's nose, you will take your empty hand and do the same motion that you have previously done with the food, and your dog should respond. If your dog does not respond to this, you may go back to the previous step. At this stage, you should always be rewarding your dog. You may also work on fading the hand signal, which simply means slowly ending the hand signal early.

The final step is to work on getting a verbal-only response. This means you have successfully faded your hand signal and only need your voice command to get your dog to respond. At this point, reinforcement should be variable, which means that you should still treat your dog for completing the command but do so at random intervals.

Questions? Comments?
Just remember to use a really awesome food treat, like some raw meat, not just something he gets on a regular basis.

As another way of training: I teach the action first before associating a word with it. I've found that a lot of people can end up repeating "sit sit sit" while trying to get their dog to sit, and the dog learns that he doesn't really have to sit until the second or third time the owner says it. Instead, I go through the lure-reward or leash pressure method to teach the correct position, until the dog consistently goes in the correct position once I start the pressure or luring, and then I end up only rewarding for the exact behavior I want after he understands what I'm wanting. Once I have the behavior perfect, I start to associate the word and/or hand signal with it, and I have found that I get more precise results when I'm associating the word with the exact behavior that I want. It takes a bit longer, but then I don't have to deal with sloppy sits or repeating a command multiple times, and I can still use hand signals or verbal commands, depending on what I want the dog to do.

I am a former lobbyist ask me anything.

I was what you would call a "gun for hire" or a contract lobbyist as opposed to an "in-house" lobbyist. I generally worked for whomever I was contracted to - firearms/second amendment, tobacco, cigars, a few corporate interest groups. I was not someone who lobbied only for one group but there were groups that I would not lobby for under any circumstances.
The specific interest groups that I would or would not work for or do you mean the ones that I have worked for in the past?
would you lobby against something you were personally in support of? would it take more money?

It depends what it was and how much was being offered. Honestly there will be things I will never lobby for, sex offenders reduced sentencing, more restrictions on lobbying, restrictions on tobacco, ect.
i imagine there are lobbyist who would take that work though?
Of course there are always people who share some values or are willing to ignore values for enough money.
You mentioned in a comment that there were some companies you would never work for. What's the motive behind that?

There are some people or organizations that I have such personal bias or sour history with that I would never work for them and would even go as far as working against them if collateral circumstances allowed.
Are you allowed to name any of those companies?

There are some clients that I am allowed to name and some that I can not. The companies I will not work for are primarily unions, with the exception of Fire or Police, anyone that advocates for higher taxes, anyone that advocates for any form of socialization or any progressive cause.
If somebody wanted to work as lobbyist, what are the requirements? Certain educational attainment or just having great network of people?

Honestly, there are no requirements to be a lobbyist. It depends how well connected you are and what your skill set is; there is also the question of if you want to be Government Relations, Hired Gun Lobbyist, Issue Lobbyist, Think Tank Personnel, or a lobby firm.

Typically a lobbyist has a Public Policy Masters or Law Degree if they are a Federal Lobbyist or an exceptional background and network or they have a political science degree and start as a research analyst.

Law or political science degree makes sense to ensure you wont cross the legal boundaries.

Follow-up question, I have this biased ideas that lobbying is tantamount to bribing or blackmailing government officials to sway to make a "friendlier" policies and decision for the benefit of the lobbyist. To some extent they are the ones creating the policy and the government officials just putting their signature in it. Is this what lobbying is all about?

Political Science was usually just because people who wanted to study something they liked it does not really give you any advantage. There is a distinct advantage for a law degree and it has nothing to do with regulatory legalities that is just knowing three or four penal code items and the chapter of lobbying regulations. The law degree is so that you can understand how to read legalease and write the language for a legislative bill or amendment.

No, most lobbyists do not have the sway to get a bill drafted that the rep did not agree with already; they help mainly with language and the implications of language in the law. The main point of a lobbyist to to go to a congressmen and explain the negative implications to an industry of a provision in a bill and recommend a new provision or an amendment to rectify the bill.

Bribing and blackmailing doesn't apply to congress for the most part. When I say that I mean that if I threaten to tell people you did something when you did that is reporting a fact not a threat. When I support a candidate that shares my belief that is free speech and issues driven politics.

I can tell the actual story without revealing who I am explicitly so I will say I was smoking a cigar with a friend of a friend and my personal history came up and he told me I should come work in the political field with him and that was that.
Depends, what city are you in and what is your work experience - I'm assuming you want more than just a cigar.
